p: Rashid Ali was the son of Sayyid Abd al-Wahhab al-Gailani and belonged to a prominent Baghdad family whose name points to an origin in Gilan in Iran and which traces its ancestry to the Prophet Muhammad; he also descended from Circassian governors of the Ottoman period. He studied at the law school in Baghdad and practised as a lawyer before entering politics.

In 1924 Yasin al-Hashimi made him minister of justice in his first government, and he was elected president of the Chamber of Deputies in 1925 and 1926. Both men were nationalists opposed to any British part in Iraq's internal politics. They rejected the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty signed by the government of Nuri as-Said in 1930 and formed the Party of National Brotherhood. Gaylani was prime minister for the first time from March to November 1933.

He returned to the premiership on 31 March 1940, after the early death of King Ghazi, when Emir Abdul-Illah was regent for the four-year-old Faisal II. Gaylani refused Allied troops passage through Iraq, rejected calls to break with Fascist Italy and sent his justice minister, Naji Shawkat, to Ankara, where on 5 July 1940 he met the German ambassador, Franz von Papen. Britain imposed economic sanctions, and under pressure from the regent he resigned on 31 January 1941.

With the Golden Square he then planned to assassinate the regent, who discovered the plot on 31 March and fled. The coup followed on 1 April, and on 3 April a National Defence Government took office under Gaylani. He sent artillery against the RAF base at Habbaniya. On 2 May the base's commander struck first at the Iraqi positions; within a week the Iraqis left the escarpment, and British forces advanced through Fallujah on Baghdad. Gaylani fled to Iran on 30 May. An armistice was signed the next day, and the regent returned on 1 June. Immediately afterwards the Farhud, a violent pogrom against Jews, took place in Baghdad.

After British and Soviet forces invaded Iran on 25 August 1941 he went on to Italy and then Berlin, where Adolf Hitler received him and he was recognised as leader of an Iraqi government in exile. On Germany's defeat he found refuge in Saudi Arabia. He returned to Iraq only after the revolution of 1958 that overthrew the monarchy, plotted a revolt against the government of Abdul Karim Kassem and was sentenced to death. Pardoned in July 1961, he lived in Lebanon, where he died on 28 August 1965 at the age of 72.

notes: The article dates his second premiership 'March 1940 to February 1941' in the lead and his resignation to 31 January 1941 in the text; I used the latter.
The article spells the name Gaylani and Gailani; I used Gaylani as the entry does.
Left out for space: his exile to 'Ana in 1938 and the Mufti's letter of introduction carried by Shawkat.
